name: Fluted Pumpkin
description: A vigorous climbing vine grown for iron-rich dark leaves and protein-rich seeds. It is one of Nigeria's most widely eaten indigenous vegetables, and the seeds are milled into egusi. It is dioecious, so some vines never bear pods.

statesProvenance.note: Compiled from the crop's established growing belt and state lists already on the site. State-level suitability has not yet been confirmed with each ADP; treat as a starting list, not a guarantee.

climate.note: Grown all year. The rainfed crop runs roughly March to November; the dry-season crop runs November to March under irrigation, or on residual moisture in valley bottoms.

soil.texture: Moist, well-drained, fertile soil; responds strongly to organic matter.
soil.note: NIHORT gives pH 6.0-7.5. The old GRO record said 5.5-6.8; that figure was not sourced and is corrected here.

planting.nursery: Sow in beds under shade or in nursery trays, 30-50 cm between rows on beds or 10-15 cm in trays. Transplant at the 6-leaf stage, when the vine is about 70 mm.
planting.note: Seed rate is 10,000-20,000 seeds per hectare depending on target plant density. The dry-season system is a different crop technically: dense, unstaked, short-cycle.

water.note: Rainfed crop depends on steady rainfall. Dry-season production uses irrigation, residual moisture in valley bottoms, or streams. Do not assume the crop needs twice-weekly watering in all systems; that depends on soil and season.

nutrition.note: Apply about 20 t/ha of poultry manure before planting. Where that is not practical, apply 25-50% pre-plant and supply the rest with a split NPK top-dress. Two split applications of 80-90 kg N/ha have given about 10 t/ha of vine. These are per-hectare figures: scale to the plot, and do not copy them to a 0.1 ha garden.

problems.name: White leaf spot
problems.control: Stake early so leaves stay off the soil, remove badly infected leaves, avoid overhead watering, and rotate away from cucurbits.

problems.name: Root-knot nematodes
problems.control: Use healthy seed, rotate with cereals, add organic matter, and destroy infected roots. NIHORT's guide lists carbofuran (Furadan) for this; it is banned in Nigeria and must not be used.

pestsAndDiseases.ipmFirst: Start with staking, clean seed, rotation and sanitation. The old guide's chemical list is not a safe default: check every active ingredient against NAFDAC before publication, and prefer cultural control on a small plot.

harvest.note: Cut vines with a clean knife about 5 cm above a node so the plant can sprout again; leave enough leaves to support regrowth. Harvest in the early morning or late evening while plants are turgid. Pods mature 90-115 days after flowering; seed kept in the pod stays viable 3-5 months, or about 3 weeks in the lower fridge compartment.

postHarvest.note: Keep bundles cool and damp, out of the sun, and transport under the same conditions. Do not wash before storage. Harvest only what you can sell or eat within a few days; leafy ugu wilts fast.

safety.pesticidePolicy: No pesticide is recommended on this page. If a pest problem justifies a chemical, use only a product registered by NAFDAC for that crop on the date of use, follow the label dose, wear the stated PPE, and observe the pre-harvest interval. Re-check registration before every season.
safety.ppe: Long sleeves, trousers, gloves, boots, eye protection and a nose/mouth cover when handling or spraying any agrochemical. Wash work clothes separately and bathe after spraying.
safety.preHarvestInterval: Follow the product label. Never harvest leaves inside the stated interval; leafy crops are eaten raw or lightly cooked and residues are not removed by washing.
safety.bannedInputsNote: Carbofuran (Furadan), paraquat, atrazine and chlorpyrifos are banned or phased out by NAFDAC. Banned products still circulate in markets, so buy only from a licensed dealer and check the label.
safety.wastewaterWarning: A 2022 Okigwe survey found 26.7% of dry-season growers irrigating with wastewater. That is a food-safety risk for a leaf crop eaten fresh; do not present it as a recommendation.

practices.claim: The rainfed crop is planted with the rains (roughly March-November); dry-season ugu is grown November-March under irrigation or in valley bottoms.
Stake after the first cut, about 4-6 weeks after planting, and drive stakes at least 30 cm into the soil. Staking keeps leaves off the soil, reduces white leaf spot, and makes harvesting easier.
Do not treat scattered early rains in southern Nigeria as the start of the season. NiMet's 2026 forecast warns that early rains are not onset and gives state-level onset dates.

Most smallholder ugu in the southeast is grown by women on farms averaging about 0.7 ha, and the crop is profitable but inputs are used inefficiently: labour, seed and manure tend to be over-applied while land and capital are under-used.

In Enugu, 63% of ugu farmers had no extension contact in the previous year, and most sold through village or local markets (56.9%), village squares (27.6%) and roadside stands (16.2%); only 3.6% sold through cooperatives.
Dry-season ugu in Okigwe was profitable in 2021/22, but growers depended on streams and wastewater for irrigation and faced high input costs, poor roads and no irrigation facilities.
NIHORT's ugu guide still recommends Furadan (carbofuran) for nematodes. NAFDAC banned carbofuran outright in 2023, so that section of the guide must not be copied.

economics.caveat: Reported per farm for one dry season (mean farm 0.54 ha). Naira values are from 2022 and are not current prices. Use the method, not the number: recalculate with today's input and market prices.

openQuestions: Do southeast growers cut at 5 cm above a node, or leave 30 cm as the old GRO page said? Measure regrowth on both in the 2027 season.
Which staking method (single stake, tripod, trellis, table) gives the best labour return at 0.25-0.5 ha?
How much does bamboo stake replacement actually cost per season, and is there a cheaper local material?
Does wastewater irrigation change leaf contamination levels enough to justify a public warning beyond the survey finding?
Which local seed sources give reliable germination, and what is the real cost per 1,000 viable seeds?
